Al-Shahrastānī believes the question took a new form when later Muʿtazilites began reading the works of philosophers.
He says that they eventually reduced all of God’s attributes to two: that God is knowing and powerful.
They then argued that these were essential attributes.
Al-Jubbāʾī described them as two ways of considering the one eternal essence: one as knowing and one as powerful.
Abū Hāshim described them as two “states” of the essence.
Abū al-Ḥusayn al-Baṣrī went further and tended to reduce them to a single attribute, knowledge.
Al-Shahrastānī comments that this was essentially the position of the philosophers.
What concerns us now is how Muʿtazilite thinking about the attributes moved from its simpler form to a more philosophically complex one.
Once the Muʿtazilites moved beyond Wāṣil’s early and relatively simple explanation, they began to analyze the attributes used of God in the Qurʾān.
They concluded that some of these attributes are negative. They do not add any positive quality to God.
For example, calling God eternal means that he has no beginning.
Calling him one means that he has no partner.
Other attributes, however, seem to affirm something positive: power, knowledge, life, and will.
This is what al-Shahrastānī means when he says that they eventually reduced all the attributes to God’s being “knowing” and “powerful.”
They regarded these as positive attributes, while treating the others as negative in the sense just explained.
The negative attributes caused no real problem for them, because they do not add anything to God’s essence.
The positive attributes did create a problem.
How can God possess these attributes?
Do they add something to his essence?
Or are they identical with his essence?
The Muʿtazilites chose the second answer.
These attributes are not something other than God’s essence. They are the essence itself.
There is only one reality: God’s essence.
So when we say that God is powerful, knowing, living, and willing, what we mean is:
God is powerful through his own essence, not through a separate power.
He is knowing through his own essence, not through a separate knowledge.
He is living through his own essence, not through a separate life.
He wills through his own essence, not through a separate will.
They adopted this interpretation because saying that God is powerful through a power, or knowing through a knowledge, appears to produce two things in every case.
There would be knowledge and one who knows.
Power and one who has power.
The result would be a multiplication of eternal realities according to the number of attributes.
That would mean either several gods or several eternal beings.
Both possibilities contradict the principle of divine unity: one eternal God.
There were differences among the Muʿtazilites over exactly how the unity of essence and attributes should be understood. But these were differences of form rather than substance.
Al-Shahrastānī points to some of them in the passage we quoted earlier.
Al-Jubbāʾī treated knowledge and power as essential attributes and said that God’s essence could be considered in two respects: as knowing and as powerful.
Abū Hāshim—ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyya—described knowledge and power as two “states” of the divine essence.
But this difference does not change the basic position.
In both cases, God’s attributes are identical with his essence. They are not additions to it and do not exist separately from it.
This is also what al-Qāḍī ʿAbd al-Jabbār meant in the passage quoted earlier:
“The Muʿtazilites unanimously agree that the world has an eternal creator who is powerful, knowing, and living, but not through separate meanings.”
In other words, these attributes do not refer to meanings that exist in addition to God’s essence.
The great Muʿtazilite theorist Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf (135–227 AH / 751–842 CE) introduced a new formula for the problem of the attributes.
In substance, however, it still remained within the general Muʿtazilite idea that God’s essence and attributes are one.
“knows through a knowledge that is himself, has power through a power that is himself, and lives through a life that is himself.”
Al-Shahrastānī sees a difference between this formula and the earlier Muʿtazilite statement that God is “knowing without knowledge,” and so on.
In his view, al-ʿAllāf’s formula affirms an essence that is itself an attribute—or an attribute that is itself the essence.
The earlier formula, by contrast, appears simply to deny the attribute altogether.

“borrowed this view from the philosophers”—meaning the Islamic philosophers—“who believed that God’s essence is one and contains no multiplicity of any kind. The attributes are not meanings existing beyond the essence and residing in it. Rather, they are the essence itself, and they can be understood either as negations or as necessary implications.”
By “negations,” al-Shahrastānī means, for example, that describing God as knowing can be understood as denying ignorance of him.
The same applies to the other attributes.
By “necessary implications,” he means that affirming knowledge of God necessarily implies the denial of ignorance.

A few lines later, however, al-Shahrastānī argues that once al-ʿAllāf treats these attributes as different aspects of the divine essence, they become effectively the same as the Christian hypostases or Abū Hāshim’s “states.”
Al-Ashʿarī, meanwhile, believes that al-ʿAllāf took his view of the attributes from Aristotle.

We will briefly move ahead of our argument here to examine these two claims: al-Shahrastānī’s claim that al-ʿAllāf’s attributes are essentially the same as the Christian hypostases, and al-Ashʿarī’s claim that al-ʿAllāf took his view from Aristotle.
First, the general direction of al-ʿAllāf’s thinking on the attributes remains within the broader Muʿtazilite approach.
That approach does not fit the Christian idea of the hypostases, with its complex structure that is difficult to separate from the ideas of plurality and incarnation.
Both ideas are far removed from Muʿtazilite thought in general and from al-ʿAllāf’s thought in particular.
Second, it is difficult to accept al-Ashʿarī’s claim that al-ʿAllāf took his theory of the attributes from Aristotle.
Aristotle did not discuss the problem of divine attributes in this form.
What he discussed was divine thought and the object of that thought.
Aristotle argued that divine thought cannot have anything other than the divine essence itself as its object.
He based this on another argument: divine thought cannot be directed toward an object less noble than the divine essence.
Since God is the highest of all beings, and his existence is the highest form of existence, Aristotle concluded that there are things the divine intellect cannot reasonably think about.
The divine intellect must therefore think itself.
Because the divine intellect is the highest reality, its thought becomes thought thinking itself—intellect thinking intellect.
This shows the difference between Aristotle’s starting point and al-ʿAllāf’s.
In fact, we can also find an important difference in where their arguments lead.
As we will see shortly, al-ʿAllāf affirms that God has the attribute of knowledge.
The implications of this position connect God’s knowledge with particular existing things.
Continuing this discussion, we now return to al-ʿAllāf’s new formula for the divine attributes.
We need to do so because there is an important difference between his position and that of the Muʿtazilites before him, especially when it comes to God’s knowledge.
To say that God is knowing “without knowledge,” as earlier Muʿtazilites did, means denying knowledge as a distinct attribute.
From this it is possible to conclude that God knows only his own essence.
As we have just seen, Aristotle reached something close to this position.
On this view, nothing belonging to knowledge exists outside the divine essence. Knowledge and essence are one and the same.
And because the divine essence is absolute, knowledge too becomes absolute.
This can lead to the conclusion that God’s knowledge is not connected with particular things—that is, with individual beings in all their specific details.
Al-ʿAllāf, however, says that God is knowing through knowledge.
This affirms knowledge as an attribute.
From this it becomes possible to conclude that God’s knowledge is not only universal, absolute, and abstract, but also includes particular things.
If this conclusion is correct, then we have a major difference.
It places the issue at the heart of the later struggle between theological and philosophical schools over the nature of God’s knowledge.
Or does God know every individual thing and every individual event, in all its particular detail, throughout the universe and at every moment?
Some of the consequences of this debate are connected with the problem of freedom and compulsion.
If divine knowledge includes every particular event, this comes close to a doctrine of compulsion in human action.
Human actions would become like every other event and thing: eternally included within God’s knowledge.
Since the attribute and the essence are equal within the unity of God, both must also share the same eternity.
Everything and every human act would therefore have been known by God from eternity.
